questions.q: What are the three parts of a JWT, in order?
o: payload.signature.header
header.payload.signature
signature.payload.header
header.signature.payload
questions.x: A JWT is always header.payload.signature, each part Base64url encoded, joined by dots. The signature is computed over the first two parts, so it must come last.
questions.h: The signature protects the other two parts. Which two? And what must come after something it protects?

questions.q: What is the purpose of the JWT signature?
o: To compress the payload for faster transmission
To prove the token was created by a party that knows the signing key and that the content has not been modified
To encrypt the payload so only the server can read it
To encode the expiration timestamp in a tamper-proof way
questions.x: The signature is a cryptographic proof of authenticity and integrity. If the payload or header is changed, the signature no longer matches. The server verifies the signature before trusting any claim in the token.
questions.h: A token could be forged if there were no check on its integrity. What does the signature allow the server to check?

questions.q: Which JWT claim controls token expiration?
o: sub
iss
exp
iat
questions.x: exp (expiration time) holds a Unix timestamp in seconds. A correctly implemented server rejects any token with an exp in the past. iat (issued at) records when the token was created. sub identifies the subject (user).
questions.h: The claim name is a three-letter abbreviation. What word means 'valid only until a certain time'?

questions.q: Can the JWT payload be read by anyone who intercepts the token?
o: No, it is encrypted with AES-256
Yes, it is only Base64url encoded and anyone can decode it
Only if they know the signing secret
No, it is compressed and not human-readable
questions.x: Base64url is encoding, not encryption. The payload is fully readable by anyone with the token. Sensitive data should never be stored in a JWT payload unless the token is also encrypted (JWE).
questions.h: Try running echo 'eyJzdWIiOiJ3aWVuZXIifQ' | base64 -d in a terminal. Is a key needed?

questions.q: What is the difference between a stateless JWT and a server-side session?
o: A JWT must be stored in a database while a session uses a cookie
A JWT carries all needed data in the token itself so the server needs no storage, a server-side session stores data on the server and the client only holds a session ID
JWTs are only for mobile apps while sessions are for web apps
JWTs expire automatically while sessions last forever
questions.x: Stateless JWTs make the server horizontally scalable because no shared session store is needed. The tradeoff is that a JWT cannot be invalidated before its expiration without extra infrastructure like a token blocklist.
questions.h: What does 'stateless' mean for the server? Does it need to remember anything between requests when using JWTs?
